Neonatal Pygmy hippopotamuses emerge at a remarkably modest mass, with newborns weighing approximately 5000 grams [Wwb = approximately 5000 grams] at parturition. This initial body size, representing less than three percent of the adult weight, is typical of ungulates that adopt a hiding strategy during the early post-natal period. The low birth mass relative to the maternal investment underscores a life-history trade-off between producing a sufficiently developed calf and the energetic constraints of a solitary, forest-dwelling frugivore. Field observations from the Sapo National Park in Liberia indicate that these neonates are capable of standing and nursing within hours of delivery, a precocial pattern that enhances their survival in predator-rich environments. The relatively small size at birth also influences subsequent growth trajectories, as the calf must nearly double its weight in the first few months to reach the weaning threshold. Comparative data from other forest ungulates suggest that the 5000 gram [Wwb = 5000 gram] birth weight of Hexaprotodon liberiensis is consistent with its low basal metabolic rate and the correspondingly slow pace of early development, a pattern that persists throughout its life history.

The reproductive strategy of the Pygmy hippopotamus is characterized by exceptionally low annual fecundity, which aligns with its extended lifespan and prolonged developmental periods. Females produce a single calf per litter [N_R_i = single calf per litter], and inter-birth intervals are long, with most reproductively active individuals experiencing only one parturition every two years [F_R_i = one parturition every two years]. This yields a maximal reproductive rate equivalent to 0.4 calves per year under optimal captive conditions. This meager output is among the lowest recorded for any artiodactyl of its body size and reflects the species' specialization on stable, resource-poor forest habitats. The energetic cost of producing a single, well-developed offspring at the observed birth weights is substantial, effectively limiting the frequency of reproductive events. In captivity, the inter-birth interval can be as short as twelve months, but field data from the Taï National Park corroborate the slower pace observed in the wild, confirming that extrinsic ecological factors such as food availability and predation risk further constrain the already low intrinsic capacity for population increase.

Gestation in the Pygmy hippopotamus spans approximately 199 days [tg = approximately 199 days], a figure that falls within the range expected for a mammal of its size but is notably shorter than the gestation of its larger congener, the common hippopotamus at a temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. This duration has been consistently documented across several captive breeding programs operating at a physiological temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C], which corresponds to the species' core body temperature. The relatively modest gestation length, combined with the single-offspring litter size, implies a considerable investment of maternal resources per unit time. Following parturition, the offspring remains entirely dependent on the mother for nutrition during an extensive lactation period. Calves begin nibbling solid vegetation after a few weeks but continue to suckle regularly. The process of weaning, defined as the cessation of milk ingestion and the achievement of full nutritional independence from the mother, occurs at approximately 198 days after birth [tx = approximately 198 days after birth] under the same thermal regime of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. This prolonged period of maternal care is integral to the juvenile's acquisition of foraging skills necessary for survival in the dense understory of West African forests.

The attainment of sexual maturity in the Pygmy hippopotamus is a significantly delayed event relative to its total lifespan. Puberty in females has been recorded at approximately 1278 days after birth [tp = approximately 1278 days after birth], corresponding to roughly three and a half years of age, a developmental milestone observed in zoo populations maintained at a constant core temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. Males may require an even longer period to reach reproductive competence, with some captive records indicating that testicular descent and spermatogenesis are not completed until around 1644 days, though this figure requires further confirmation through longitudinal studies. This delayed sexual maturation is consistent with the species' overall slow life-history strategy, which prioritizes somatic growth and body mass accumulation before allocating resources to reproduction. The long interval between birth and puberty also contributes to the low population turnover rates observed in this species, making it particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic pressures such as habitat fragmentation and hunting. The extended pre-reproductive period is a common trait among large-bodied, long-lived mammals inhabiting stable, low-mortality environments.

Maximal longevity in the Pygmy hippopotamus is considerable, with the oldest documented individuals surviving for approximately 42.3 years [am = approximately 42.3 years] in captivity at a temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. This lifespan, when converted to a daily equivalent, amounts to roughly 15,439.5 days under standard conditions. The adult body mass associated with this extended lifespan is substantial, with fully grown individuals attaining an ultimate wet weight of 240,000 grams [Wwi = 240,000 grams]. Field records indicate a considerable range in adult size, with most mature animals falling between 180 and 275 kilograms, variation that likely reflects local differences in habitat quality and food availability across their fragmented West African range. The combination of a long life, late maturity, low fecundity, and high offspring investment places the Pygmy hippopotamus firmly at the slow end of the mammalian life-history continuum, a strategy that has proven successful in stable forest ecosystems but renders the species exceptionally sensitive to environmental perturbation.
